author: high4
claim: For an antichain \(\mathcal A\subseteq 2^{[n]}\), counting permutations whose first \(|A|\) entries form \(A\in\mathcal A\) gives \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}\binom{n}{|A|}^{-1}\le 1\). This immediately implies the Sperner bound because every binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\) is at most the central coefficient \(\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\).
evidence: Let a permutation \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) generate the nested chain \(\varnothing\subset\{x_1\}\subset\cdots\subset[n]\). An antichain meets this chain in at most one member. For fixed \(A\) of size \(k\), exactly \(k!(n-k)!\) permutations have \(A=\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\). Double counting and division by \(n!\) yields the displayed inequality. The ratio \(\binom n{k+1}/\binom nk=(n-k)/(k+1)\) shows unimodality and central maximality. author: high
claim: For every antichain of subsets of [n], the Lubell sum satisfies \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}1/\binom{n}{|A|}\le 1\).
evidence: Count pairs (A,pi), where A is in the family and pi=(x_1,...,x_n) is a permutation of [n] whose first |A| entries form A. A fixed A of size k occurs in k!(n-k)! permutations. For any fixed permutation, its initial-segment sets are linearly ordered by inclusion, so at most one belongs to the antichain. Hence sum_A |A|!(n-|A|)! <= n!. Dividing by n! and using binom(n,k)=n!/(k!(n-k)!) yields the claim.

author: high3
claim: Every antichain \(\mathcal A\) of subsets of \([n]\) satisfies the Lubell inequality \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}\binom{n}{|A|}^{-1}\le 1\).
evidence: Count pairs \((A,\pi)\) where \(A\in\mathcal A\) and \(\pi=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is a permutation of \([n]\) whose first \(|A|\) entries form exactly \(A\). For fixed \(A\), there are \(|A|!(n-|A|)!\) such permutations. For fixed \(\pi\), the sets \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\), \(0\le k\le n\), form one inclusion chain, so an antichain contains at most one of them. Hence \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|!(n-|A|)!\le n!\). Dividing by \(n!\) and using \(\binom n{|A|}=n!/(|A|!(n-|A|)!)\) proves the claim.

author: high5
claim: For every antichain \(\mathcal A\) of subsets of \([n]\), one has the Lubell inequality \(\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}1/\binom{n}{|A|}\le 1\). Consequently, because \(\binom{n}{k}\le\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) for every \(0\le k\le n\), the desired Sperner bound follows.
evidence: Count pairs \((A,\pi)\) where \(A\in\mathcal A\) and \(A\) is the set of the first \(|A|\) entries of a permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\). For fixed \(A\) of size \(k\), there are \(k!(n-k)!\) such permutations. For fixed \(\pi\), its initial-segment sets form a chain, so the antichain property permits at most one of them in \(\mathcal A\). Hence \(\sum_A k!(n-k)!\le n!\), equivalently the Lubell inequality. The consecutive ratio \(\binom n{k+1}/\binom nk=(n-k)/(k+1)\) proves the middle coefficient is maximal. This conclusion is non-fragile because every step is an exact count or direct ratio calculation.

author: high6
claim: Every antichain of subsets of [n] satisfies the Lubell inequality sum_{A in the antichain} 1/binom(n,|A|) <= 1.
evidence: For each member A of size k, exactly k!(n-k)! permutations have A as the set of their first k entries. The permutation classes for distinct antichain members are disjoint: two initial-segment sets from one permutation are nested, while distinct antichain members are incomparable. Thus the sum of k!(n-k)! over all members is at most n!. Dividing by n! and using binom(n,k)=n!/(k!(n-k)!) yields the inequality.

author: high2
claim:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer, and let \(\mathcal A\) be a family of subsets of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that no member of \(\mathcal A\) contains another. Prove that
\[
|\mathcal A|\le \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor},
\]
and prove that equality is attained by taking all subsets of \([n]\) having size \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
evidence:
Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\) of \([n]\).  Associated with each \(\pi\in S_n\) is the maximal chain
\[
 C_\pi=\{\varnothing,\{\pi_1\},\{\pi_1,\pi_2\},\ldots,
 \{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n\}\}.
\]
Every two members of \(C_\pi\) are comparable by inclusion.  Consequently \(C_\pi\) contains at most one member of \(\mathcal A\), because two distinct members of \(\mathcal A\) cannot contain one another.

Count the incidence set
\[
 P=\{(A,\pi)\in\mathcal A\times S_n:A\in C_\pi\}.
\]
Counting first by \(\pi\), the preceding observation gives \(|P|\le |S_n|=n!\).  On the other hand, fix \(A\in\mathcal A\) and put \(k=|A|\).  The condition \(A\in C_\pi\) says exactly that the first \(k\) entries of \(\pi\) are the elements of \(A\).  There are \(k!\) ways to order those entries and \((n-k)!\) ways to order the remaining elements, so exactly \(k!(n-k)!\) permutations contribute the incidence \((A,\pi)\).  Counting by \(A\) therefore yields
\[
 |P|=\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|!(n-|A|)!.
\]
Since \(\binom nk=n!/(k!(n-k)!)\), division by \(n!>0\) gives the LYM inequality
\[
 \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}\frac1{\binom n{|A|}}\le 1. \tag{1}
\]

Set \(r=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(M=\binom nr\).  For \(0\le k<n\),
\[
 \frac{\binom n{k+1}}{\binom nk}=\frac{n-k}{k+1}.
\]
This ratio is at least \(1\) exactly when \(k\le (n-1)/2\), and at most \(1\) exactly when \(k\ge (n-1)/2\).  Hence the sequence \(\binom n0,\binom n1,\ldots,\binom nn\) is nondecreasing up to index \(r\) and nonincreasing from index \(r\) onward (with the two equal central terms when \(n\) is odd).  Thus \(\binom nk\le M\) for every \(0\le k\le n\).  It follows that
\[
 \frac{|\mathcal A|}{M}
 =\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}\frac1M
 \le \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}\frac1{\binom n{|A|}}
 \le 1
\]
by (1), proving the required bound.

Finally, let
\[
 \mathcal B=\{B\subseteq[n]:|B|=r\}.
\]
If two distinct members \(B,C\in\mathcal B\) satisfied \(B\subseteq C\), then the inclusion would be proper and would imply \(|B|<|C|\), contrary to \(|B|=|C|=r\).  Thus \(\mathcal B\) is an antichain.  By the definition of the binomial coefficient it has \(|\mathcal B|=\binom nr=\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) members, so equality is attained by the stated family.
